course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Matrix Inverses and Determinant Properties
sessionGoal: Students should be able to use inverses and determinant properties without turning every problem into a long row-reduction problem.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start by saying: an inverse undoes a matrix, and a determinant tells us if an inverse exists.
Do Problem 1 slowly because it connects inverse matrices to solving systems.
Use Problem 2 to practice determinant shortcuts.
Use Problem 3 to emphasize parameter values that make a matrix singular.
Point students to Practice Lab Sections 4-5 afterward.
sayThisFirst: A matrix has an inverse only when its determinant is nonzero.
If A is invertible, then Ax=b has exactly one solution: x=A^{-1}b.
Do not compute an inverse unless the problem actually asks for it.
Determinant properties are shortcuts. Use them before doing arithmetic.
boardPlan: Write: invertible \(\Leftrightarrow \det(A)\neq 0 \Leftrightarrow Ax=b\) has one solution for every \(b\).
Do Problem 1: inverse plus solving Ax=b.
Do Problem 2: determinant properties only, no row reduction.
Do Problem 3: find when a parameter makes \(\det(A)=0\).
commonMistakes: Writing \(\det(A+B)=\det(A)+\det(B)\), which is not a rule.
Trying to invert a matrix before checking whether the determinant is zero.
Mixing up A^{-1}b with bA^{-1}; vectors go on the correct side.
notationWarnings: Use A^{-1}, not 1/A, for a matrix inverse.
Write \(\det(A)\), not \(|A|\), if students might confuse it with absolute value.
For a 2 by 2 inverse, keep the sign changes in the off-diagonal entries.

problems.title: Use a 2 by 2 inverse to solve a system
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: first check the determinant. If it is nonzero, the inverse exists and we can use x=A^{-1}b.

drawInstructions: Draw Ax=b as: A sends unknown x to known b.
Draw A^{-1} as the step that sends b back to x.
Emphasize that the inverse exists because \(\det(A)=1\), not 0.

walkthrough.label: Check that the inverse exists
walkthrough.latex: \[\det(A)=2(3)-1(5)=6-5=1.\] Since the determinant is nonzero, \(A^{-1}\) exists.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide by the determinant. Here the determinant is 1, so it looks invisible.
Swapping the wrong entries in the 2 by 2 inverse formula.
Multiplying b on the wrong side.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 4 for inverses and transformations.

problems.title: Use determinant properties instead of row reduction
problems.studentPromptLatex: Suppose \(A\) is a \(3\times 3\) matrix with \(\det(A)=-3\). Compute \(\det(2A^T A^{-1})\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: this is not asking us to know A. We only need determinant rules.

drawInstructions: Write the expression as a product of three determinant pieces.
Point out that A^T and A have the same determinant.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 4 for determinant properties.

problems.title: Find parameter values that make a matrix non-invertible
problems.studentPromptLatex: For what values of \(k\) is \[A(k)=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&k-1&1\\0&3&k+1\end{bmatrix}\] not invertible?
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: not invertible means determinant equals zero. We do not need the inverse.

drawInstructions: Highlight the first column because it makes expansion easy.
Write \(\det(A(k))\) as a 2 by 2 determinant after expansion.
Mark the values where the determinant becomes zero.

walkthrough.label: Expand using the first column
walkthrough.latex: The first column has two zeros, so \[\det(A(k))=1\cdot\det\begin{bmatrix}k-1&1\\3&k+1\end{bmatrix}.\]

commonMistakes: Forgetting that not invertible means singular.
Expanding along a hard row or column instead of using the zeros.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 4 for determinants and invertibility.

qualityControlNotes: Checked A inverse: det=1 and A^{-1}b=(-1,6).
reviewSummary: Session 10 emphasizes inverses as tools and determinant properties as shortcuts.

open.title: Undo buttons and shortcuts
say: An inverse matrix is an undo button: A⁻¹ takes every output of A back to the input it came from.
Today we use inverses to solve systems, and learn the determinant rules that let you skip huge computations. Shortcut first, arithmetic second.

ask.q: If A stretches everything by a factor of 3 in some direction, what must A⁻¹ do?
ask.a: Shrink by a factor of 3 in that same direction.

idea.title: Determinants multiply, so inverses divide
say: Think of the determinant as the area scale factor. Doing B then A scales area by det B and then det A, so det(AB) = det A · det B.
An inverse undoes the scaling, so det(A⁻¹) = 1 / det A. And transposing doesn't change the scaling: det Aᵀ = det A.
One trap: scaling the whole matrix. For an n × n matrix, det(cA) = cⁿ det A, because every one of the n directions gets stretched by c.
draw: Draw a unit square, then an arrow labeled B to a parallelogram (area det B), then an arrow labeled A to a bigger one (area det A · det B).
Draw a 3 × 3 cube doubled in all three directions and write 'volume × 2³ = 8'.

ask.q: A is 3 × 3 with det A = 2. What is det(3A)?

launch.say: Find A⁻¹ with the 2 × 2 formula, then solve Ax = b using it.
circulate: Check the swap-and-negate pattern: swap a and d, negate b and c.
Make sure they multiply A⁻¹b, not bA⁻¹.

askFirst.q: What should you check before writing any inverse?

steps.say: det A = 6 − 5 = 1. Nonzero, so the inverse exists.

ask.q: What would det A = 0 have meant for Ax = b?
ask.a: No inverse: either no solution or infinitely many.

steps.say: Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by det = 1.

ask.q: How do you check an inverse quickly?
ask.a: Multiply A by it and see if you get I.

steps.why: x = A⁻¹b is the matrix version of dividing both sides by a number. It only works when the inverse exists.

si10-p1.meaning: A sends (−1, 6) to (4, 13), and A⁻¹ sends it back. Because det A ≠ 0, that's the only input that works.

ifStuck.if: a student swaps b and c instead of a and d
ifStuck.then: multiply their 'inverse' by A; it won't give I.

si10-p1.transition: That inverse was cheap. Next: a problem where computing anything explicitly would be a waste, because the rules do all the work.

launch.say: det A = −3 for a 3 × 3 matrix. Find det(2AᵀA⁻¹). No matrix given, just rules.
circulate: Watch for det(2Aᵀ) = 2 det A. It's 2³.

askFirst.q: Which three rules will you need?
askFirst.a: det(cB) = cⁿ det B, det Aᵀ = det A, and det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, plus det(product) = product of dets.

steps.say: The determinant of a product is the product of determinants: det(2Aᵀ) · det(A⁻¹).

ask.q: Why can we split it like this?

steps.say: 2Aᵀ is 3 × 3, so the 2 comes out cubed: 8 det Aᵀ.

ask.a: The 2 multiplies all three rows, and each row contributes one factor of 2.

steps.why: This is the most common determinant-rule mistake on exams.

steps.say: det Aᵀ = det A = −3, and det(A⁻¹) = 1/(−3) = −1/3.

ask.q: Sanity check: what is det(AᵀA⁻¹) alone?
ask.a: 1: they cancel. So the whole answer is just 2³ = 8.

si10-p2.meaning: Aᵀ scales volume by det A, and A⁻¹ undoes exactly that, so together they cancel. Only the factor 2 in all three directions is left: volume × 8.

ifStuck.if: a student wants to invent a matrix with det −3
ifStuck.then: it would work, but ask them to try the rules first; it's three lines.

si10-p2.transition: Last one: find the parameter values that make a matrix non-invertible.

launch.say: For which k is A(k) NOT invertible? Use the zeros.
circulate: Who expanded down column 1? That's the fast way.

ask.q: How many bad values of k could there be?
ask.a: As many as the roots of the determinant polynomial.

steps.say: Expand down column 1: only the top 1 contributes, times the lower-right 2 × 2 block.

ask.q: Why do the other two terms vanish?
ask.a: Their entries in column 1 are zero.

ask.q: Check k = 2: are two rows or columns dependent?
ask.a: Rows 2 and 3 become (0, 1, 1) and (0, 3, 3): row 3 is 3 times row 2.

si10-p3.meaning: Two special values of k tilt the rows into dependence and flatten the volume to zero. For any other k, the matrix can be undone.

ifStuck.then: it still works but is longer; show the column-1 shortcut side by side.

wrap.write: Invertible ⟺ det ≠ 0 ⟺ Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b. det(AB) = det A det B, det Aᵀ = det A, det A⁻¹ = 1/det A, det(cA) = cⁿ det A.

exit.q: Give three equivalent ways to say A is invertible.
exit.a: det A ≠ 0; a pivot in every column; Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b (also: columns independent).

exit.q: Why does det(cA) depend on the size of A?
exit.a: c scales every one of the n rows, contributing n factors of c.
